newsitem.title: CANADA: French Quebec power pivotal in Canada election.
newsitem.headline: French Quebec power pivotal in Canada election.

text.p: As Canada's election campaign races toward the June 2 finish line, the pivotal role of French-Canadian power in federal politics is taking center stage in an emotional debate over national unity.

Preston Manning, leader of the right-wing Reform Party, based in Western Canada, outraged other party leaders with a series of recent attacks on prominent politicians from French-speaking Quebec -- including Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien and Conservative leader Jean Charest.

A Reform television advertisement broadcast in English showed three French-Canadian party leaders along with separatist Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard and called for "a voice for all Canadians, not just Quebec politicians."

A group representing the roughly one million French-Canadians living outside Quebec called the ads insulting and slanderous. Quebec separatists branded the ads racist and urged broadcast regulators to ban them.
Manning was unrepentant, saying the ads might help the party's election fortunes in British Columbia.
Reform's campaign tactic may have stemmed from Quebec politicians' domination of federal politics for the past 30 years, although Quebec has only one-quarter of Canada's 29 million people,
"In a country where 25 percent of the population speaks French, political competence means being bilingual," said Jean Pare, publisher and editor-in-chief of Montreal-based news magazine L'actualite.

Manning does not speak French, which severely limits his national political ambitions. By contrast, with the exception of New Democratic Party leader Alexa McDonough, who speaks halting French, the other three major party leaders are all bilingual French Quebeckers.

Prime Minister Jean Chretien, 63, whose Liberals have a comfortable lead in opinion polls over the Conservatives, is a Quebec native. So is 38-year-old Charest, whose surge in opinion polls came at the expense of the separatist Bloc Quebecois, led by Gilles Duceppe, another French Quebecker.

In the 1993 election, the Bloc won 54 of the 75 seats in Quebec, the only province in which it fields candidates. That was enough to place second to Chretien's Liberals and edge out Reform to form the official opposition in Canada's British-style parliament.

Charest is the most popular federal party leader in Quebec and Manning has a strong following in Western Canada. But Chretien remains the leader Canadians outside Quebec most want as prime minister, even if he speaks English with a heavy French accent.

By contrast, since Liberal Pierre Trudeau was first elected prime minister in 1968, Quebec has shunned federal leadership from outside the province. Canada has had a fluently bilingual prime minister from Quebec for 28 of the past 29 years.

"Quebeckers do not seem ready to accept political leadership from outside Quebec, while people from outside Quebec seem willing to accept leadership from Quebec. It's a remarkable phenomenon," said Peter Leslie, political affairs professor at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario.
Since Trudeau, French Canadians' role in Ottawa has gone beyond defending Quebec's interests to directing the federal government's most important functions.

In 1977, Chretien became Canada's first French-Canadian finance minister. In his current cabinet, Quebeckers hold five important posts, including those of finance minister and Treasury Board president.
